title: Let the children come (Matthew 19:1–15)
hookLine: his friends shoo the children away; he puts his hands on their heads
tomorrow: a rich young man kept every rule. why did he walk away sad?

lines: A TODDLER LOOSE AT A WEDDING.
cards: A toddler loose at a wedding. A baby crying in the quiet part of a service. A kid asking a loud question at a museum.
There's usually someone ready to shush them. In Matthew, it's Jesus' own friends.
He has just answered a hard question about marriage, "What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder," and the grown-ups are still taking that in.
"Then were there brought unto him little children, that he should put his hands on them, and pray: and the disciples rebuked them." Why? Matthew doesn't say.

teach.h: WHO DOES THE KINGDOM BELONG TO?
teach.b: Here's the old question: who does the kingdom belong to? Jesus answers it with the interruption. "Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven."
Suffer, in the King James, means let. Let them come.

teach.h: HE LAID HIS HANDS ON THEM.
teach.b: And then Matthew shows rather than tells: "he laid his hands on them, and departed thence." No speech about them. A hand on each head, and then the road.
Now a neighbor who knows that gesture well.

teach.h: FRIDAY NIGHT: AS EPHRAIM AND MANASSEH.
teach.b: In the Torah, the old man Jacob lays his hands on the heads of his grandsons, Ephraim and Manasseh, and blesses them, and says that Israel will bless by their names: "God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh."
In Jewish homes that keep the custom, parents still say those words over their sons on Friday night, at the Shabbat table, and bless their daughters by the names of Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah.
Hands on a child's head, and a blessing: that much the two traditions share.
And one honest difference. The Jewish blessing comes from a parent, at home, week after week, in words from the Torah.
In Matthew, strangers' children are carried to a teacher on the road, and the ones trying to keep them away are his own followers.

how: Some churches invite children forward for a blessing with a hand on the head, and some Christian parents bless their children at bedtime; in Jewish homes that keep the custom, parents bless their children on Friday night.

o: a rule that children must be baptized as babies
a call for parents to send kids to Sunday school
Jesus' welcome to children his friends turned away

Genesis 48:20, Jacob's blessing over his grandsons, still said in some Jewish homes on Friday night.

Matthew records one sentence, then: he laid his hands on them, and departed thence.

games.q: at a Jewish friend's Friday dinner, her parents put their hands on each child's head and bless them. your little cousin whispers: is that like when Jesus blessed the kids?
o: in one way: hands on a child's head and a blessing. theirs is Jacob's words, from parents, at home.
yes, it's exactly the same blessing, only said in Hebrew instead of English.
no, it has nothing in common with anything in the Gospels.
games.why: the gesture is shared: a hand on a child's head. the setting differs: a parent's weekly blessing in words from Genesis, and a teacher on the road blessing strangers' children.

practice: Count on your fingers the children in your life: kids, nieces and nephews, neighbors, the ones you coach or teach, the child you used to be. Give each finger a name and a moment of plain thanks.
If one of them is near you today, a hand resting on their head, the way Jacob did and the way Jesus did, says it without a speech.

wordCard.voice: Let the children come. Suffer them, forbid them not: the interruption is who the kingdom is made of.

orig.note: Greek: let, allow; the word behind suffer in Matthew 19:14.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: of such is the kingdom, said over the very kids his friends turned away. Until tomorrow.
